claims.text: Increasing atomic size mismatch in single-phase high-entropy alloys increases local lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion caused by atomic size mismatch impedes dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion increases yield strength.
The proposed comparison can be conducted in either FCC or BCC disordered single-phase solid solutions.
Composition will be systematically varied to produce a series with progressively increasing atomic size mismatch.
Matching grain size, phase purity, chemical homogeneity, and processing conditions isolates the effect of lattice distortion.
Alloys with greater atomic size mismatch will have higher hardness than the low-mismatch baseline.
Alloys with greater atomic size mismatch will have higher yield strength than the low-mismatch baseline.
In situ TEM will show lower dislocation mobility in alloys with greater lattice distortion.
A baseline alloy with minimal atomic size mismatch will have negligible lattice distortion.
A baseline alloy with minimal atomic size mismatch will present lower barriers to dislocation motion.
The proposed relationship is expected to hold when strengthening contributions from grain boundaries, precipitates, and secondary phases are controlled.
The proposed relationship is limited to moderate temperatures and strain rates where thermally activated mechanisms do not dominate.
Local chemical ordering may independently influence dislocation dynamics.
Minor processing variations and other strengthening mechanisms may affect the measured hardness and strength.
Failure of hardness and yield strength to increase consistently with atomic size mismatch would falsify the proposed governing relationship.
Failure to observe reduced dislocation mobility with increasing lattice distortion would falsify the proposed mechanism.
